Subject: SIG follow-up: multi-tenant KV cache and GPU boundary questions

Connor -

Thanks again for the quick SIG intake last week. Our InfoSec team had a couple of follow-ups specific to Dedicated/Dual-tenant (hosted) configurations that came up while we were filling out Section 3 of the SIG:

- Can you confirm whether the in-memory KV cache (used to store prefix/kv caches for active sessions) is namespaced per-tenant so that keys from Tenant A cannot be accessed by Tenant B? Any implementation notes on namespace enforcement would help.

- For your Dedicated offering, is GPU assignment exclusive at the process/node level (i.e., can two tenant workloads ever share the same GPU)? If shared, what mitigations are in place for noisy-neighbor degradation or cross-tenant memory disclosure?

- We may need an architecture diagram or a redacted kube-scheduler policy to demonstrate scheduling/affinity rules for our audit. Can you tell us what artifacts you can provide?

Appreciate a short, bulletized response so I can attach it to the SIG answers. If needed, we can schedule a 30-min call this week.

Hi Elena -

Thanks - good questions. Short answers first, expanded below, and attaching a high-level diagram (isolation_diagram_v2.pdf).

- KV cache namespacing: Yes - KV entries are logically namespaced per-tenant. Each cache key is prefixed with an internal tenant namespace ID. Access controls in the serving runtime enforce a tenant boundary check before any KV read/write.

- GPU assignment for Dedicated: For Dedicated pools we provide exclusive GPU assignment at the container/process level (no co-scheduling of unrelated tenant workloads on the same GPU). For our shared-hosting (multi-tenant) clusters, we rely on strict CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES + cgroups + enforced soft quotas; noisy-neighbor mitigations include automatic throttling and fallback routing to quieter nodes or dedicated warm pools.

- Artifacts: Attached is an architecture diagram and a redacted scheduler example. We can also provide a redacted kube-scheduler policy and a short attestation letter for your audit team.

More detail (technical addendum):
- KV namespace enforcement: tenant_id is injected by the request ingress layer and immutably associated with the request context. The runtime composes the cache key as $TENANTID::$MODELID::$SESSIONID::$CACHEKEY. Enforcement points exist in the request router and the cache access layer; both validate the tenant_id token before returning any cached blocks.
- Cache persistence and eviction: Cache entries are stored in RAM on the serving node; we never serialize cross-tenant cache to shared disk. Eviction policies are per-tenant at the runtime level.
- Dedicated GPU behavior: Dedicated customers get a pinned set of GPUs mapped to their node pool. Containers/VMs in that pool are scheduled with exclusivity; we use device plugin and node labeling to guarantee no other tenant workloads are scheduled there. For fleet-level events we have an automated fallback route to compatible models in other Dedicated pools that are in the same region.

Next steps: I'll loop in Marcus with the implementation note and the redacted scheduler snippet. If you want the formal attestation, say the preferred addressee and we'll generate a signed PDF.

Elena -

Adding a short technical amendment based on your two specific asks (putting the implementation pieces into SIG-friendly language):

1) KV cache isolation (implementation notes)
- Keys: runtime prefixing with tenant UUID is mandatory. Format: tenant_uuid:model_hash:session_uuid:seq_key.
- Enforcement: both the request router (authN/authZ) and the cache access layer perform a tenant UID assertion. A mismatch rejects the request with 403.
- Memory: cache entries live in per-worker heap segments; worker processes are single-tenant scoped when running in Dedicated pools.

2) GPU isolation & noisy neighbor mitigations
- Dedicated pools: GPUs are never shared across tenant namespaces. We allocate exclusive devices via node labeling + device-plugin and the container runtime sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES accordingly. NVIDIA MPS is not used to multiplex across independent tenants in Dedicated.
- Multi-tenant/shared pools: we use resource requests/limits, burst throttles, and active telemetry to detect noisy tenants. On detection we: (a) throttle token generation for the offending tenant, (b) migrate warm sessions to other nodes, (c) surface a loud alert to ops and optionally route incoming sessions to Dedicated or burst capacity.
- Memory confidentiality: we do not expose other processes' GPU memory; GPU memory accesses are isolated by the driver/hypervisor and the CUDA runtime. We additionally zero freed buffers before reuse in our runtime when running multi-tenant processes.

Artifact suggestions for SIG: redacted kube-scheduler policy (attached as k8s-scheduling-example.yaml), a short attestation letter, and the architecture diagram. If you need an actual cluster policy, we can produce a redacted version of our scheduler policy (removing internal labels and node IDs) - that's what we typically provide during vendor reviews.

Marcus Lin
Senior SRE - Serving Infrastructure, Redwood Inference
